skills.name: Find the region that satisfies several linear inequalities

note.text:
For several inequalities at once, draw each boundary and shade the unwanted side of each. The region left clear satisfies all of them; it is often labelled R.
Example: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 4. The clear region is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4).
A point is in R only if it satisfies every inequality.
To find the whole-number points in R, check each grid point inside or on the boundary (if the boundary is included).
The greatest value of an expression such as 2x + y over R is found at a corner of R.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to find and describe the region R that satisfies several inequalities, count its whole-number points and find the greatest value of an expression in it.
Builds on: Lesson {21} (one inequality as a half plane).
Leads to: linear programming (best buys, greatest profit) in Form Five.

sections.heading: Several boundaries
sections.text:
Show x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0}, x + y ≤ {4}.
• x ≥ {0}: boundary the y-axis; shade the left side.
• y ≥ {0}: boundary the x-axis; shade below.
• x + y ≤ {4}: draw the solid line through ({4}, {0}) and ({0}, {4}); O gives {0} ≤ {4}, true, so shade the far side.
What stays clear is the triangle with corners ({0}, {0}), ({4}, {0}), ({0}, {4}). Label it R.
A point is in R only if it passes every test.

sections.heading: Points in R and best values
sections.text:
Count whole-number points row by row. For the triangle above: y = {0} gives {5} points, y = {1} gives {4}, … y = {4} gives {1}: {15} in all.
In a real problem, x and y are often numbers of items, so only whole-number points count.
To find the greatest value of {mono(2, 'x')} + y in R, try the corners: ({0}, {0}) gives {0}, ({4}, {0}) gives {8}, ({0}, {4}) gives {4}. The greatest is {8}.
Words: 'at least' means ≥, 'at most' and 'not more than' mean ≤.

key_words.meaning: the set of points that satisfy all the inequalities
a point where two boundaries meet

worked_example.problem: Show the region R given by x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0} and {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} ≤ {n}, and count the whole-number points in R.
steps: x ≥ {0}: shade the left of the y-axis. y ≥ {0}: shade below the x-axis.
Boundary {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} = {n} through ({n}, {0}) and ({0}, {n}), solid; O satisfies it, so shade the side away from O.
R is the clear triangle. Count the grid points in it, edges included: {n + 1} + {n} + … + {1}.

cards.idea: R is the clear region left when the unwanted side of every boundary is shaded.
A point is in R only if it satisfies every inequality.
The greatest value of an expression like {mono(2, 'x')} + y over R is at a corner of R.

check.prompt: R is given by x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0} and {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} ≤ {n}. Find the greatest value of {mono(p, 'x')} + {mono(q, 'y')} for points (x, y) in R with whole-number coordinates.

misconceptions.explain: ({0}, {0}) gives the smallest value, not the greatest.
{n} is the limit for {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')}, not the value of {mono(p, 'x')} + {mono(q, 'y')}.

solution: The greatest value is at a corner of R: ({0}, {0}), ({floor(n / a)}, {0}) or ({0}, {floor(n / b)}) (or a whole-number point next to the slanted edge).
Work out {mono(p, 'x')} + {mono(q, 'y')} at each and compare.

questions.prompt: R is the region where x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0} and {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} ≤ {n}. Which point is in R?

misconceptions.explain: {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} = {a * qx + b * qy}, which is more than {n}.

solution: Check each inequality for ({px}, {py}): {px} ≥ {0}, {py} ≥ {0}, {a * px + b * py} ≤ {n}.
All three hold, so the answer is {answer}.

questions.prompt: The unshaded region R satisfies x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0} and {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} ≤ {n}. How many points with whole-number coordinates are in R (edges included)?

misconceptions.explain: The edges are solid lines: points on them are in R.
x ≥ {0} and y ≥ {0} include the axes: count the points on them too.

solution: Go along each row: for y = {0}, x can be {0} up to {floor(n / a)}; then y = {1}, and so on.

questions.prompt: Which three inequalities define the unshaded region R in the graph?

misconceptions.explain: R contains points near O, and O gives {0} ≤ {n}: the sign is ≤.
R lies to the right of the y-axis and above the x-axis: x ≥ {0}, y ≥ {0}.
Check the intercepts: the line meets the x-axis at x = {n / a}, so the x coefficient is {a}.

solution: R is to the right of the y-axis (x ≥ {0}) and above the x-axis (y ≥ {0}).
The slanted line meets the axes at ({n / a}, {0}) and ({0}, {n / b}): it is {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} = {n}, and R is on O's side.

questions.prompt: A trader in Kumba buys x bags of rice and y bags of beans. She buys at least {r} bags of rice, at least {s} bags of beans, and at most {t} bags in all. Which inequalities describe this?

misconceptions.explain: x counts rice (at least {r}) and y counts beans (at least {s}).

solution: 'At least {r}' means {r} or more: x ≥ {r}. Likewise y ≥ {s}.
'At most {t} in all' means x + y ≤ {t}.
